headline: UVM Medical Center labor deal heads to ratification vote after strike threat
dek: A tentative two-year agreement could avert a walkout by roughly 3,300 support and technical workers, but the contract terms remain private until members vote.
body: A tentative two-year labor agreement at the University of Vermont Medical Center is headed to a ratification vote, putting a possible strike on hold at Vermont’s largest hospital while workers review a contract whose terms have not been released. The agreement was announced Tuesday by AFT Vermont, according to [Vermont Public’s report](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-10-06/support-staff-techs-reach-tentative-deal-with-uvmmc). Union members are scheduled to vote from Wednesday through Sunday, Oct. 11.

The deal covers two bargaining groups representing roughly 3,300 employees at the Burlington medical center. The [VTDigger account](https://vtdigger.org/2026/10/06/uvm-medical-center-unions-reach-tentative-agreement-in-contract-negotiations/) describes the support-staff unit as including licensed nursing assistants and schedulers, while the technical-professionals unit includes jobs such as laboratory and sterilization technicians. Those positions are not interchangeable with doctors or registered nurses, but they are part of the day-to-day workforce that keeps patient care, testing, cleaning, transport and scheduling moving through a large academic hospital.

The agreement follows months of bargaining that began in April. Last week, 82% of voting members authorized union leaders to call a strike, a step that gave negotiators leverage but did not itself start a work stoppage, [Vermont Public reported](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-10-02/support-staff-techs-at-uvmmc-authorize-a-strike). The two sides reached the tentative deal before the unions issued a formal 10-day strike notice, according to [Vermont Business Magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/october/06/unions-and-uvmmc-administration-reach-tentative-agreement).

Safe staffing and job security were central issues in the negotiations. Union representatives sought more say in determining how many employees are assigned to hospital floors, while workers across the University of Vermont Health Network have experienced three rounds of layoffs in two years, Vermont Public reported. The hospital and unions have not disclosed whether the tentative contract changes staffing rules, protects particular positions or alters wages and benefits.

That missing detail is important. A tentative agreement is not a ratified contract, and the public announcement does not establish what members will receive or what management agreed to change. [VTDigger reported](https://vtdigger.org/2026/10/06/uvm-medical-center-unions-reach-tentative-agreement-in-contract-negotiations/) that representatives on both sides declined to provide the terms before the vote. Until members approve or reject the deal, the labor dispute remains unresolved even though the immediate prospect of a strike has receded.

The negotiations also unfolded during a difficult financial period for the medical center. Vermont Public reported that hospital chief executive Stephen Leffler recently told regulators the medical center could lose about $75 million this year. The same report said the hospital has faced pressure from regulators and lawmakers to reduce health-care costs, while its expenses continue to rise. Those financial claims come from the hospital’s own statements to regulators and do not, by themselves, explain the terms of the tentative agreement.

For patients and families, the near-term effect is continuity: the tentative deal means the support and technical workers are not preparing an announced walkout while the ratification process runs. It does not guarantee that staffing levels will improve, that layoffs will stop or that service costs will fall. Those outcomes depend on the contract language, the membership vote and the hospital’s broader financial decisions.

The ratification vote is the next decision point. A yes vote would turn the tentative agreement into the governing contract for the two units, while a no vote would leave the parties to determine their next bargaining step. The agreement’s wage, staffing and job-security provisions are expected to become clearer only after the union membership has completed its vote, making the result and the eventual contract terms the next developments to watch in Burlington.
location: University of Vermont Medical Center, Burlington, Vermont
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: UVM Medical Center unions take tentative deal to vote
seoDescription: A tentative two-year UVM Medical Center labor agreement could avert a strike by roughly 3,300 support and technical workers in Burlington.
